According to that supplied draft, the commitments included a large deportation program, closing the border, ending birthright citizenship, imposing tariffs and pardons tied to the January 6 attack. It also says the review distinguished campaign statements from actions a president could take alone and noted possible limits from Congress and the courts. These points are retained only as drafting inputs: the linked AP tracker did not yield readable content in the prior packet, and the live extraction attempt in this review returned HTTP 502. The material does not identify a particular promise row, deadline, implementation status or outcome. The frozen record's March 4, 2026 date does not match the supplied draft's reference to a January 2025 report, and no evidence in the packet resolves that mismatch. This draft therefore makes no finding about promise fulfillment, changing criteria, repeated review cycles, public credibility costs or institutional risk. It is an unverified description of what prior supplied material attributes to AP, pending an accessible source and event date.

frozen_original.title: Trump Hosting Foreign Heads of State at Mar-a-Lago for Paid Memberships — Emoluments
frozen_original.synopsis: Throughout early 2025, Trump conducted significant foreign policy meetings and hosted foreign heads of state at Mar-a-Lago, his private Florida club where membership fees were reported to have increased dramatically after his return to the presidency. Foreign government officials and lobbyists reported pressure or incentives to purchase Mar-a-Lago memberships and stay at Trump-branded properties. Ethics watchdogs filed new emoluments clause complaints citing documented payments from foreign governments to Trump-owned properties. The pattern was seen as an extension of first-term practices that courts had been prepared to rule unconstitutional before the cases became moot. Democrats demanded financial disclosure of foreign payments to Trump properties, which the administration refused.

primary.title: Supplied Allegations of Paid Foreign Access at Mar-a-Lago Remain Unverified
primary.description_short: The supplied record alleges foreign officials faced pressure to buy Mar-a-Lago memberships or Trump-property stays; those claims remain unverified.
primary.description_medium: The supplied account alleges that foreign officials and lobbyists faced pressure or incentives to buy Mar-a-Lago memberships or stay at Trump-branded properties in early 2025, followed by emoluments complaints and disclosure demands. Forbes reported foreign officials from at least eight countries visiting Mar-a-Lago, but did not document purchases, pressure, the alleged complaints, or a disclosure refusal.
primary.description_long: During early 2025, the supplied record alleges that Donald Trump held foreign-policy meetings at Mar-a-Lago, his private Florida club, after membership fees reportedly rose following his return to the presidency. It further alleges that foreign officials and lobbyists faced pressure or incentives to buy memberships or stay at Trump-branded properties. The synopsis says ethics watchdogs filed new Foreign Emoluments Clause complaints about payments from foreign governments to Trump-owned properties, and that Democrats sought financial disclosure while the administration refused. These statements are retained as claims in the supplied record; the packet does not name the officials, lobbyists, watchdogs, complaints, or requested disclosures, and provides no contracts, receipts, correspondence, or response document. Forbes reported in January 2025 that officials from at least eight foreign countries had visited Mar-a-Lago since Trump’s reelection. That reporting documents visits, but it does not say the visitors bought memberships or stays, were pressed to do so, or made payments to Trump businesses. It also does not substantiate the claimed new complaints or refusal. This draft preserves the alleged sequence for internal review while separating it from the limited, sourced fact about visits. It reaches no conclusion that payments occurred or that a violation was found.
primary.date_basis: 2025-01-25 is carried from the frozen record; the alleged chronology and event start are not independently established.

frozen_original.title: Bessent Treasury Kills Financial Institution Stress Tests
frozen_original.synopsis: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to eliminate mandatory stress tests for major financial institutions, removing key safeguards put in place after the 2008 financial crisis to ensure banks could withstand severe economic downturns without requiring taxpayer bailouts. The stress tests had been a cornerstone of post-crisis financial regulation and had been credited with strengthening the banking system. Economists warned the elimination increased the risk of another financial crisis requiring massive government intervention.

blockers: The frozen title and synopsis say Scott Bessent or Treasury eliminated mandatory stress tests for major financial institutions in March 2025. No source in the supplied packet or targeted search supports that action; the Federal Reserve continued its annual 2025 stress-test cycle, publishing scenarios and later results.

The sourced 2025 actions belong to the Federal Reserve Board, not Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Replacing the alleged Treasury action with the Federal Reserve’s separate annual test would substitute a different event rather than correct the stated event.

research_attempts.query: March 2025 Scott Bessent Treasury eliminate mandatory Federal Reserve stress tests major banks 2025 annual stress test scenarios
research_attempts.result: Official Federal Reserve results included its February 5 release of 2025 annual stress-test scenarios; no result supported a Bessent/Treasury termination.

research_attempts.query: 2025 Federal Reserve Board annual stress test who conducts bank stress testing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent authority
research_attempts.result: Federal Reserve background material states that the Board conducts supervised-bank stress tests; returned sources did not support an action by Bessent or Treasury.

research_attempts.query: Federal Reserve 2025 annual stress test results August 2025 large banks stress test release
research_attempts.result: Found the Federal Reserve’s June 27, 2025 release of annual test results for 22 banks, directly inconsistent with the frozen claim that the annual regime had been eliminated.
Succeeded (HTTP 200). The Board says it released hypothetical scenarios for its annual stress test on February 5, 2025, with 22 banks to be tested.
Succeeded (HTTP 200). The Board published annual test results June 27, 2025 and reported all 22 tested banks remained above minimum CET1 requirements.
Both source pages returned extracted text with status success; the February scenarios and June results confirm continuation of the Fed’s annual process.

source_fact_map.fact: The Federal Reserve Board released hypothetical scenarios for its annual stress test on February 5, 2025; the release says 22 banks would be tested.
source_fact_map.quote: The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday released the hypothetical scenarios for its annual stress test
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
February 05, 2025

### Federal Reserve Board releases the hypothetical scenarios for its annual stress test

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday released the hypothetical scenarios for its annual stress test, which helps ensure that large banks can lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. Additionally, the Board released two hypothetical elements designed to probe different risks through its “exploratory analysis” of the banking system. The exploratory analysis will not affect bank capital requirements.

The Board’s annual stress test evaluates the resilience of large banks. This year, 22 banks will be tested.

source_fact_map.fact: The Federal Reserve Board reported 2025 annual stress-test results on June 27, 2025 for 22 banks.
source_fact_map.quote: All 22 banks tested remained above their minimum CET1 capital requirements during the stress scenario
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
June 27, 2025

### Federal Reserve Board’s annual bank stress test showed that large banks are well positioned to weather a severe recession

The results of the Federal Reserve Board’s annual bank stress test showed that large banks are well positioned to weather a severe recession.

All 22 banks tested remained above their minimum CET1 capital requirements during the stress scenario, after absorbing total projected hypothetical losses of more than $550 billion.

frozen_original.title: DHS compiling lists of journalists, lawyers, and professors critical of Trump
frozen_original.synopsis: The Department of Homeland Security compiled dossiers on journalists, lawyers, and academics who publicly criticized the Trump administration, in a targeted effort to suppress dissent. Reports revealed that DHS was systematically cataloguing individuals across various professions who had voiced criticism of Trump policies, creating watch lists that could be used to target these individuals through immigration enforcement, travel restrictions, or other government mechanisms.

primary.title: Unverified supplied allegation that DHS compiled dossiers on Trump critics
primary.description_short: The frozen record alleges DHS compiled dossiers on critics, but the sources found describe public employee lists created by a private nonprofit.
primary.description_medium: The frozen record alleges DHS compiled lists of journalists, lawyers, and professors critical of Trump for possible immigration or travel retaliation. The claim is not established by the supplied packet. Reporting located here instead describes lists of federal workers created by the American Accountability Foundation, a private group, including a DHS-focused list naming immigration judges, lawyers, advisers, and analysts. Those reports do not establish a DHS-created dossier or government retaliation.
primary.description_long: The frozen record alleges that, beginning in February 2025, DHS compiled dossiers or watch lists of journalists, lawyers, and professors critical of Trump, potentially enabling immigration or travel retaliation. This card preserves that allegation only as supplied; neither the source packet nor the sources accessed here establish that DHS compiled or used such a list. Reporting located during review describes related but distinct activity: The Guardian reported that the American Accountability Foundation, a private nonprofit, had created a DHS-focused watchlist and said it included immigration judges, lawyers, policy advisers, and analysts. The New York Times separately reported that the same group published lists of federal employees, including a newer list covering federal health agencies. These reports identify a private organization’s public lists, not a DHS file of outside journalists and professors or government retaliation. They do not verify the frozen record’s February 1 date, and they cannot be substituted for its exact allegation. Keep this internal draft unpublished until a contemporaneous DHS document or credible report matching the claimed authorship, targets, date, and purpose is available.

source_fact_map.fact: The Guardian described a private foundation’s DHS-focused watchlist and said it included immigration judges, lawyers, policy advisers, and analysts.
source_fact_map.quote: The DHS list includes immigration judges, lawyers, policy advisers and analysts.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Founded in 2020, the group received $100,000 in funding for its first watchlist—focused on the Department of Homeland Security—from the Heritage Foundation. The foundation called its list initiative “Project Sovereignty 2025” and said it was aimed at exposing the people behind the scenes who were advancing Biden’s border policies. The DHS list includes immigration judges, lawyers, policy advisers and analysts.

source_fact_map.fact: The New York Times reported that the American Accountability Foundation published lists of federal employees, including workers at DHS, and that a later list covered federal health agencies.
source_fact_map.quote: The foundation previously published “watch lists” of workers at the Defense, Education and Homeland Security Departments.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The list was compiled by the American Accountability Foundation, a small right-wing nonprofit that was founded in 2020 to oppose Biden administration policies and nominees. Since Mr. Trump’s election, the group has stepped up its targeting of specific federal workers—some of them career employees with little power—that it believes oppose his agenda. The foundation previously published “watch lists” of workers at the Defense, Education and Homeland Security Departments. This latest list, published on an affiliated website, includes workers from federal health agencies like the National Institutes of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
